topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Natural selection, antibiotic resistance and interpreting change

sections.heading: Start with inherited variation
sections.body: Individuals in a population differ. Some differences result from genetic variation and may be inherited; others result mainly from environmental conditions. Mutation can introduce new alleles, while sexual reproduction reshuffles existing genetic information. Natural selection requires relevant variation before the selective outcome. An organism does not generally create a useful inherited mutation because it recognises a need. Identify the particular trait and how it affects survival or reproductive success in the stated environment.

sections.heading: Link survival to reproduction over generations
sections.body: A selection pressure changes the relative chances of survival and reproduction. Individuals with a beneficial inherited trait are more likely to contribute alleles to the next generation. Over many generations, the relevant allele may become more common. Survival alone is not the full explanation: the inherited difference must influence contribution to later generations. The advantageous trait depends on conditions, so an allele beneficial in one environment may carry a cost or offer little advantage in another.

sections.heading: Explain antibiotic resistance without intention
sections.body: A bacterial population may contain resistant variants before treatment. An antibiotic kills or inhibits susceptible bacteria more effectively than resistant ones. Resistant survivors reproduce, so resistant bacteria can become a larger fraction of the population. Unnecessary or inappropriate antibiotic use can increase selection pressure. Antibiotics treat appropriate bacterial infections; they do not kill viruses in the same way. Discuss treatment decisions through professional guidance rather than inventing a dosing rule from an exam diagram.

sections.heading: Distinguish a changing proportion from a changing count
sections.body: If susceptible bacteria die, the resistant fraction may rise even before resistant numbers have increased substantially. A graph of percentage resistance therefore does not directly give the total bacterial population. To interpret an experiment, consider starting populations, replication, concentrations, exposure time and suitable controls. A zone of inhibition is evidence under the test conditions, not a complete clinical guarantee. Use results to support a limited conclusion and identify what additional measurements would test alternative explanations.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Populations, feeding and environmental change

sections.heading: Energy flows; nutrients cycle
sections.body: Producers transfer light energy into biomass, and consumers obtain energy by feeding. Arrows in food chains show the direction of energy transfer. At each trophic level, energy is lost through respiration, movement, waste and uneaten material; not all biomass becomes growth in the next level. Decomposers break down organic matter and return nutrients to the environment.

sections.heading: Measure a habitat without selecting a convenient result
sections.body: Quadrats estimate abundance of stationary organisms. Use random coordinates for an unbiased area sample; use a transect to investigate a gradient. Repeat sampling and calculate a mean before scaling to a larger area. Measure relevant abiotic variables such as light, temperature, water availability and pH. Correlation between abundance and a variable does not by itself establish cause.

sections.heading: Human activity changes ecological systems
sections.body: Burning fuels and deforestation affect the carbon cycle and atmospheric greenhouse gases. Fertiliser runoff may cause eutrophication: algal growth shades submerged plants, dead biomass is decomposed and decomposer respiration reduces dissolved oxygen. Sulfur dioxide contributes to acid deposition. Conservation can protect habitats, maintain biodiversity and support sustainable resource use, but decisions may involve competing social and economic priorities.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The carbon cycle follows carbon atoms through photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition and combustion. The nitrogen cycle involves a different set of transformations: fixation introduces usable nitrogen from atmospheric nitrogen, decomposers release ammonium compounds, nitrifying organisms oxidise them, and denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere. Energy flows through an ecosystem and is dissipated, while elements are recycled. A pyramid of biomass records living material at each level; it need not have the same shape as a pyramid counting organisms. Sampling conclusions should acknowledge spatial variation and the limitations of the chosen method.

topics.tip: A food-chain arrow points from the food organism toward its consumer.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Carbon and nitrogen cycles

sections.heading: Follow atoms through transformations
sections.body: Photosynthesis takes carbon from carbon dioxide into organic molecules. Feeding transfers these molecules between organisms, while respiration releases carbon dioxide. Decomposers use organic material from dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon through respiration. Combustion releases carbon from fuels or biomass. Carbon is transferred and chemically rearranged; energy entering the ecosystem is not recycled by exactly the same processes.

sections.heading: Nitrogen becomes usable through microorganisms
sections.body: Atmospheric nitrogen is not directly usable by most plants. Nitrogen fixation converts it into compounds that can enter biological systems. Decomposition releases ammonium compounds from organic nitrogen. Nitrifying microorganisms oxidise ammonium through nitrite to nitrate under suitable aerobic conditions. Plants absorb mineral nitrogen and use it in molecules such as amino acids. Denitrifying microorganisms can return nitrogen to the atmosphere, particularly where oxygen is limited.

sections.heading: Connect the cycle to farming and pollution
sections.body: Harvest removes nitrogen-containing material from an area, so nutrient replacement may be needed to sustain production. Excess fertiliser can enter waterways and contribute to eutrophication. Waterlogged soils can favour nitrogen losses through denitrification. When asked about bacteria, identify the process and chemical direction rather than saying all bacteria make nitrates. Biological cycles describe interacting populations and environmental conditions, not one universal linear chain.

topics.title: Sampling, biodiversity and ecological data

sections.heading: Match sampling to the question
sections.body: Use quadrats for organisms that can be sampled in a fixed area and a transect to investigate change along a gradient. Random coordinates reduce selection of unusually convenient or impressive locations. Repeated quadrats provide a mean and some information about variability. Systematic positions along a transect can reveal a relationship with distance, but they answer a different question from a random area survey.

sections.heading: Calculate with the sampled area
sections.body: Density is number counted divided by total area sampled. Multiply a representative density by habitat area to estimate abundance. Percentage cover can be more useful than counting individual plants when boundaries between individuals are unclear. Compare results using equal effort or an appropriate adjustment. Species richness is a count of species; biodiversity can also involve how evenly individuals are distributed among those species.

sections.heading: Evaluate the conclusion
sections.body: A correlation between light intensity and a species’ abundance does not isolate light as the cause: soil moisture or disturbance may vary too. Explain how variables are measured, consider replication and identify realistic limitations. Sampling may miss seasonal or mobile organisms. Give an estimate with a justified degree of confidence rather than claiming a quadrat survey measures every organism in the entire ecosystem directly.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Food production, biotechnology and genetic methods

sections.heading: Increase yield while considering consequences
sections.body: Greenhouses control light, temperature and carbon dioxide, but added energy and infrastructure have financial and environmental costs. Fertilisers supply mineral nutrients; biological control uses living organisms to reduce pests. Intensive livestock systems can limit movement and heat loss to improve growth efficiency, while raising welfare, disease and pollution questions that should be evaluated explicitly.

sections.heading: Use microorganisms as biological factories
sections.body: Yeast fermentation supports bread and alcoholic-drink production. Industrial fermenters maintain suitable temperature, pH, nutrients and, when needed, oxygen. Aseptic conditions reduce contamination; stirring distributes resources and heat. Pectinase can increase fruit-juice extraction and lactase can produce lactose-reduced milk. Conditions depend on the organism and desired product rather than one universal optimum.

sections.heading: Modify or copy genetic material
sections.body: Genetic engineering transfers selected genetic information between organisms, using tools such as restriction enzymes, ligase and vectors. Bacteria can be engineered to produce human insulin. Cloning generates genetically similar organisms through methods such as tissue culture or nuclear transfer. Benefits must be weighed against reduced diversity, animal welfare and unintended ecological effects. Describing a method is different from evaluating its use.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A fermenter is designed around its organism and product. Aeration is important for an aerobic process, while ethanol fermentation uses anaerobic conditions. A temperature jacket removes excess heat, and sensors allow conditions to be monitored rather than assumed. In genetic modification, a selected gene can be inserted into a vector and introduced into host cells; identifying successful transformants and controlling expression are essential steps. Clones share much genetic information, but environmental conditions and some biological details can still produce differences. Evaluation should separate evidence of a benefit from a claim that every use is equally safe or useful.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Cloning, micropropagation and evaluating biotechnology

sections.heading: Distinguish cloning from sexual reproduction
sections.body: A clone is genetically identical to its source in the relevant sense, apart from changes such as new mutations. Asexual reproduction can produce clones without gamete fusion. In plant propagation, a cutting may develop into a new plant from tissue of the parent. Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two gametes and usually produces greater variation. A clone does not have to look identical in every respect: nutrition, light, disease and other environmental conditions can change the phenotype.

sections.heading: Follow a micropropagation sequence
sections.body: Micropropagation uses small pieces of plant tissue grown under controlled sterile conditions on a suitable nutrient medium, with hormones used to support the desired growth and development. New plantlets are transferred and gradually established in appropriate growing conditions. It can produce many plants from limited starting material and preserve a selected genotype. Sterile practice matters because microorganisms can compete with or damage the growing tissue. A successful small-scale culture does not remove the need to evaluate establishment and survival after transfer.

sections.heading: Weigh uniformity against vulnerability
sections.body: A uniform crop can have predictable harvesting time and product characteristics. However, genetic similarity can make many plants vulnerable to the same pathogen or environmental change. This is a population-level trade-off, not proof that clones are always unhealthy. Compare disease status of source tissue, growing conditions, costs and the purpose of propagation. A variety chosen for high yield under controlled conditions may not be best in a drought-prone environment. Explain the trait, the benefit and the condition under which the benefit matters.

sections.heading: Evaluate animal cloning and genetic modification separately
sections.body: Cloning copies a genotype, whereas genetic modification deliberately changes genetic material using specified techniques. In nuclear-transfer cloning, the nucleus from a donor cell is associated with an egg whose nucleus has been removed, followed by development under suitable conditions. The donor nucleus supplies most of the genetic information considered in the simplified model; mitochondria and environmental effects complicate claims of complete identity. Evaluate welfare, success rates, genetic diversity, food production and conservation goals using evidence rather than treating every biotechnology as the same process.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Particles, separation and atomic structure

sections.heading: A particle model explains state changes
sections.body: Solids have particles vibrating around fixed positions, liquids have nearby particles that can move past one another, and gases have widely spaced particles moving freely. Melting and boiling overcome attractions between particles; they do not usually split the particles into atoms. Diffusion arises from random particle movement and produces net spreading down a concentration gradient.

sections.heading: Separate physical mixtures appropriately
sections.body: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid; distillation recovers a solvent or separates liquids with different boiling behaviours. Fractional distillation uses repeated vaporisation and condensation. Paper chromatography separates substances through differing movement between stationary and mobile phases. Rf compares spot travel with solvent-front travel from the same baseline.

sections.heading: Atoms and isotopes
sections.body: Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. Atomic number counts protons; mass number counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share proton number but differ in neutron number. A neutral atom has equal proton and electron numbers. Relative atomic mass is an abundance-weighted mean. Electron arrangement explains many chemical patterns; ion formation changes electrons, leaving the nucleus unchanged.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The movement of a chromatographic spot depends on its interactions with both the stationary and mobile phases. A substance more strongly retained by the stationary phase travels less far under otherwise identical conditions. Rf values are useful for comparison only when relevant conditions match. Isotopic abundance calculations use an average of isotope masses weighted by their proportions; the result does not imply that an individual atom has a fractional number of neutrons. In a heating curve for a pure substance, a plateau marks a phase change under the idealised constant-pressure conditions, while supplied energy continues to overcome attractions.

topics.tip: A chromatography baseline is drawn in pencil and kept above the initial solvent level.
topics.formula: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Bonding, structure and chemical formulae

sections.heading: Ionic and covalent bonds are different attractions
sections.body: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice. Covalent bonding is attraction involving nuclei and a shared pair of electrons. Metallic bonding is attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons. Balance ionic charges to write formulae; a neutral compound has no net charge, even though it contains charged ions.

sections.heading: Structure determines observable behaviour
sections.body: Giant ionic substances have high melting points and conduct when molten or dissolved because ions can move. Simple molecular substances often have low melting points because intermolecular attractions are weaker than their internal covalent bonds. Giant covalent structures such as diamond require many strong bonds to be broken; graphite has layers and mobile electrons. Metals conduct because delocalised electrons move through the structure.

sections.heading: Represent atoms without losing them
sections.body: A balanced equation conserves atoms of each element. Change coefficients, not chemical formulae, to balance it. State symbols distinguish solids, liquids, gases and aqueous solutions. Dot-and-cross diagrams show outer-shell electron contributions; bracket and charge ionic species correctly. For electron transfer, oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain; these occur together.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a dot-and-cross diagram, show only the required outer electrons and identify which atom contributed each shared electron. For ions, bracket the resulting ion and show its charge rather than drawing the transferred electron as a covalent bond. A small molecule can contain strong covalent bonds yet form a substance with a low boiling point because the attractions between molecules are relatively weak. Graphite conducts because some electrons are delocalised within its structure, whereas the electrons of diamond are held in its covalent bonding framework. Explain observed properties using both structure and the relevant moving or interacting particles.

topics.tip: Melting a molecular substance overcomes intermolecular attractions, not the covalent bonds inside each molecule.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Moles, concentrations and electrolysis

sections.heading: Count chemical amounts with moles
sections.body: Relative formula mass adds the relative atomic masses in a formula. Amount in moles equals mass divided by molar mass. Use balanced-equation coefficients as mole ratios, then convert to the required mass, volume or concentration. The limiting reactant is used up first. Percentage yield compares actual with theoretical yield; atom economy concerns the fraction of reactant mass incorporated into the desired product.

sections.heading: Concentration connects amount to volume
sections.body: For molar concentration, use concentration = moles/volume in dm³. Divide cm³ by 1000 before substitution. In gas calculations, use the molar gas volume specified by the question; the common school value at room conditions is 24 dm³ mol⁻¹. Empirical formulae follow the simplest whole-number mole ratio, not the simplest mass ratio.

sections.heading: Electricity drives a chemical change
sections.body: Electrolysis requires mobile ions. Cations move to the negative cathode, where reduction occurs; anions move to the positive anode, where oxidation occurs. A molten binary ionic compound produces its elements. In aqueous solutions, water-derived species compete, so identify the ions and the electrode rules before predicting products. In electroplating, the object to be coated is the cathode.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A limiting-reactant calculation first converts both starting amounts to moles. Divide each by its balanced-equation coefficient to compare available reaction units; the smaller value limits product formation. In electrolysis, electrons move through the external circuit and ions carry charge through the electrolyte. At an electrode, a half-equation must balance both atoms and net charge. For copper deposition, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu describes reduction. An aqueous electrolyte may generate a product from water-derived ions, so predictions must consider all relevant species and the stated electrode materials.

topics.tip: Never insert a volume in cm³ into n = cV when c is in mol dm⁻³.
topics.formula: n = m/M; c = n/V

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Empirical formulae and molecular formulae

sections.heading: Mass ratios are not atom ratios
sections.body: A formula records relative numbers of atoms. Start from masses or percentage composition and divide each element’s mass by its relative atomic mass. The resulting mole values are proportional to atom numbers. Dividing by the smallest value gives a ratio that may need multiplying to remove simple fractions. Do not round a ratio near 1.5 directly to 2; check whether multiplying all parts by two gives a sensible whole-number ratio.

sections.heading: From empirical to molecular information
sections.body: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio. A molecular formula gives the actual atom numbers in a molecule. Divide the molecular relative mass by the empirical-formula mass to obtain an integer multiplier, then multiply every subscript. Ionic giant structures are described by their formula ratio rather than a molecular formula for an isolated molecule in the same way.

sections.heading: Interpret an experiment critically
sections.body: A metal-oxide experiment can use the change in mass as oxygen gained, under the stated assumptions. topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Electrolysis: ions, electrodes and balanced half-equations

sections.heading: Identify the mobile charged particles
sections.body: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive chemical change in an electrolyte. An ionic substance conducts when its ions can move, as in a melt or suitable aqueous solution; in a solid ionic lattice the ions are not free to move through the material. Positive ions move towards the negative cathode and negative ions towards the positive anode. Electrons travel through the metal wires and electrodes. Do not explain conduction through the liquid as electrons flowing freely between dissolved ions.

sections.heading: Distinguish molten from aqueous systems
sections.body: A molten binary ionic compound contains the ions of that compound, making the product prediction relatively direct. An aqueous solution includes species associated with water as well as the dissolved substance. At an inert cathode, a sufficiently unreactive metal may be deposited; otherwise hydrogen is commonly formed in the school model. At an inert anode, a halogen may form from a suitable halide solution, while oxygen is often formed when halide is absent. Concentration and electrode material matter, so state the given electrolyte and conditions before predicting products.

sections.heading: Balance atoms and charge in half-equations
sections.body: Reduction is electron gain and occurs at the cathode. For example, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu shows copper ions becoming copper atoms. Oxidation is electron loss and occurs at the anode; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ balances both chlorine atoms and charge. Check the total charge on each side separately from the atom count. Electrons belong in a half-equation but cancel when appropriately combined oxidation and reduction half-equations are added. The electrode sign in an electrolytic cell should not be confused with the sign conventions for every other type of cell.

sections.heading: Explain active electrodes and observations
sections.body: In copper purification or plating, copper electrodes can take part in the reactions. At a copper anode, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ removes copper into solution; at the cathode, copper ions gain electrons and deposit. With inert electrodes in copper sulfate solution, anode chemistry differs. Observations should include an appropriate deposit, gas or electrode-mass change and connect it to the particle process. Use only the teacher’s approved apparatus: some electrolysis products require controlled handling and should never be identified by directly inhaling an unknown gas.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Limiting reactants, gas volumes, yield and atom economy

sections.heading: Use the equation as a mole ratio
sections.body: A balanced equation gives reacting amounts in moles, not usually equal masses. Convert each given mass using amount = mass/molar mass, then compare the available amounts with the coefficient ratio. The limiting reactant is used up first and sets the theoretical amount of product. An excess reactant remains after the limiting reactant is consumed. Looking only for the smaller mass is unreliable because molar masses and equation coefficients can differ substantially.

sections.heading: Connect moles with measured gas volumes
sections.body: For gases at the same temperature and pressure, volume ratios follow mole ratios. In school calculations at room temperature and pressure, use the molar gas volume supplied in the question, often 24 dm³/mol. Convert cm³ to dm³ before using a relation expressed in dm³/mol. A gas collected over time may include experimental losses or water vapour depending on the method; distinguish an ideal stoichiometric calculation from the limitations of a real measurement.

sections.heading: Separate theoretical and actual yield
sections.body: The theoretical yield follows from the balanced equation and limiting reactant. The actual yield is the amount isolated or measured in the experiment. Percentage yield = actual yield/theoretical yield × 100. Product loss during transfer, incomplete reaction or side reactions can lower yield. An apparent yield above 100% suggests issues such as a wet or impure product or an incorrect calculation. A high yield does not by itself show that a process makes little waste or has low energy demand.

sections.heading: Evaluate atom economy as a different measure
sections.body: Atom economy compares the formula mass of the desired product, with its stoichiometric coefficient included, to the total formula mass of the reactants as written in the balanced equation. It describes how much of the reacting material is theoretically incorporated into the desired product. It is distinct from percentage yield, which concerns how much product is actually obtained relative to the theoretical amount. In evaluating a manufacturing route, also consider energy, feedstock availability, hazards, separation, recycling and the value or disposal of by-products.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Chromatography, solubility and choosing a separation method

sections.heading: Choose the method from the property difference
sections.body: A separation works because substances differ in a physical property such as solubility, boiling point or attraction to phases. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; it does not remove a dissolved salt. Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid by changing the amount of solvent or temperature under suitable conditions. Simple distillation can collect a solvent from a solution, while fractional distillation separates suitable mixtures with different boiling ranges. Explain which substance is collected and why the selected property difference makes that possible.

sections.heading: Explain movement in paper chromatography
sections.body: A solvent is the mobile phase and the paper provides the stationary phase in a simplified school model. Components move differently because of their differing interactions with the phases. Start with a small spot on a pencil baseline above the solvent level. If the sample is submerged, it can dissolve directly into the solvent reservoir rather than produce the intended separation up the paper. Mark the solvent front promptly before it becomes hard to see. Ink is unsuitable for the baseline because its own components may move and interfere.

sections.heading: Calculate and interpret Rf values
sections.body: The Rf value is the distance moved by a substance from the baseline divided by the distance moved by the solvent front from the same baseline. It has no units. Measure to the centre of a reasonably defined spot. Compare Rf values only under equivalent conditions such as the same solvent and stationary phase. A matching Rf supports identification when combined with an appropriate reference, but it does not prove uniqueness: different substances may have similar values under one set of conditions.

sections.heading: Evaluate purity and experimental limitations
sections.body: More than one separated spot indicates more than one detectable component in the sample under the method’s conditions. One spot does not guarantee absolute purity because components may overlap or fail to be detected. A sharp melting point or characteristic boiling behaviour can provide additional evidence for a pure substance in suitable conditions. Distinguish a measurement that supports a conclusion from proof beyond all alternatives. Repeat a poor separation using smaller spots, a better solvent system or suitable detection, with teacher guidance.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Periodic trends, air and water

sections.heading: The table organises electron patterns
sections.body: Elements in a group have related outer-electron arrangements and similar chemistry. Across a period the proton number increases. Group 1 metals react with water to produce hydroxides and hydrogen; reactivity generally increases down the group as the outer electron is more easily lost. Group 7 halogens form negative ions; a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution.

sections.heading: Atmospheric gases have distinctive uses and tests
sections.body: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and variable water vapour. Oxygen supports combustion and relights a glowing splint. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop in a suitable test. Carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy. Combustion in insufficient oxygen can produce poisonous carbon monoxide and particulates. Complete hydrocarbon combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.

sections.heading: Water treatment is a sequence of processes
sections.body: Sedimentation and filtration remove suspended material; disinfection reduces harmful microorganisms. Dissolved salts may require desalination, for example through distillation or membrane methods, with energy and infrastructure costs. Pure water is a single substance; potable water is safe to drink but may contain dissolved substances. Chemical tests must distinguish an observed result from the conclusion drawn from it.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In Group 1, increasing distance and shielding make the outer electron easier to remove down the group, despite increasing nuclear charge. For halogens, the attraction for an incoming electron generally weakens down the group, so their displacement trend is opposite. When identifying gases, specify the test material and observation: a glowing splint relights in oxygen, while carbon dioxide makes limewater cloudy. Water treatment may disinfect without removing dissolved ions. Desalination and sterilisation solve different problems, and potable water does not need to be chemically pure.

topics.tip: Reactivity trends down Group 1 and Group 7 go in opposite directions.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Metals, extraction and corrosion

sections.heading: Reactivity predicts competing reactions
sections.body: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound. The reactivity series also helps predict reaction with water, steam and dilute acids. Metal oxides can often be reduced by carbon if the metal is less reactive than carbon; more reactive metals generally require electrolysis of a suitable molten compound. Extraction method therefore depends on chemical reactivity and economic conditions.

sections.heading: Extraction involves chemical and practical decisions
sections.body: In iron extraction, carbon monoxide reduces iron oxide while limestone-derived material removes acidic impurities into slag. Aluminium extraction uses electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, reducing operating temperature. The carbon anodes are consumed because oxygen formed there reacts with them. Recycling metals often needs less energy than extraction from ore, but collection and sorting also have costs.

sections.heading: Rusting needs water and oxygen
sections.body: Iron corrosion can be reduced by barriers such as paint, grease or plastic. Galvanising adds a zinc coating that acts both as a barrier and as sacrificial protection. A more reactive attached metal preferentially oxidises. Alloys contain more than one element; differently sized atoms can disrupt the layers and make sliding more difficult, often increasing hardness.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An alloy is not simply a mixture that must always be harder; its composition and processing determine the useful properties. For many common alloys, different atomic sizes hinder layer movement compared with a pure metal. In extraction questions, separate reduction of the metal compound from removal of impurities. In aluminium production, cryolite lowers the operating temperature of the electrolyte mixture, reducing energy demand compared with melting pure aluminium oxide. Sacrificial protection needs an electrical connection and a suitable environment for the corrosion cell; a disconnected zinc object nearby does not automatically protect iron.

topics.tip: A barrier coating and sacrificial protection are different mechanisms.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Acids, salts and chemical analysis

sections.heading: Neutralisation is a reaction of ions
sections.body: Acids produce H⁺ in aqueous solution and alkalis produce OH⁻. Neutralisation forms water from these ions. Acid + metal forms a salt and hydrogen; acid + carbonate forms a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates and nitric acid nitrates. Strong versus weak describes ionisation, whereas concentrated versus dilute describes amount per volume.

sections.heading: Choose the correct salt-preparation route
sections.body: For a soluble salt from an insoluble base, add excess base to warm acid, filter off unreacted solid and crystallise the filtrate. For an acid and soluble alkali, a titration identifies the reacting volumes without leaving excess reagent. An insoluble salt can be made by precipitation from two suitable soluble solutions, followed by filtration, washing and drying.

sections.heading: Observations identify substances
sections.body: Flame tests give characteristic colours for selected metal ions. Sodium hydroxide can form characteristic hydroxide precipitates with metal ions. Acidified silver nitrate tests for halides; acidified barium solution tests for sulfates. Carbonates release carbon dioxide with acid. Ammonium ions release ammonia when warmed with alkali; ammonia turns damp red litmus blue. State the reagent, conditions and actual observation.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A titration measures the volume needed for reactants to reach the required stoichiometric relation. Rinse a burette with the solution it will contain, record readings consistently, and add dropwise near the endpoint while mixing. Repeat to obtain concordant titres rather than averaging a rough result indiscriminately. For a pure salt from an acid and alkali, the measured quantities can be reacted again without indicator. Analytical observations should distinguish precipitate colour from gas evolution. Acidification in some ion tests removes interfering ions; the choice of acid must not introduce the ion being tested.

topics.tip: Do not heat a crystallising solution to complete dryness if the aim is well-formed crystals.

topics.title: Titration calculations and soluble salts

sections.heading: Use the reacting ratio
sections.body: A titration combines measured volumes with a balanced chemical equation. Convert volumes to dm³ when using mol dm⁻³. Calculate the moles in the known solution, use the equation’s coefficient ratio, then find the concentration of the unknown. An acid-base reaction is not always a 1:1 mole relationship; sulfuric acid reacting fully with sodium hydroxide is a useful counterexample.

sections.heading: Make the measured volume reliable
sections.body: An initial rough titration locates the approximate endpoint. Later trials approach it carefully with mixing and dropwise addition near the change. Use suitable concordant titres according to the question or laboratory guidance. Read the burette consistently and calculate delivered volume from the difference between readings. Rinse apparatus appropriately so unwanted water or residues do not alter the effective concentrations.

sections.heading: Prepare a salt without indicator contamination
sections.body: When both acid and base are soluble, adding an excess leaves contamination that cannot simply be filtered away. A titration establishes the required amounts. A preparation can then use measured quantities without indicator before concentration and crystallisation. The actual method and indicator depend on the chemicals and school instructions. topics.title: Ion tests and evidence from observations

sections.heading: Test a clear hypothesis
sections.body: Analytical tests identify evidence for particular ions under stated conditions. Flame tests can identify selected metal ions, such as sodium’s yellow or copper’s characteristic blue-green flame. Avoid transferring contamination between samples. Sodium hydroxide can form coloured metal hydroxide precipitates, while some white precipitates dissolve in excess reagent. State the observation before inferring the ion.

sections.heading: Use suitable reagents for negative ions
sections.body: A halide test commonly uses nitric acid followed by silver nitrate: chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide cream and iodide yellow. A sulfate test uses an appropriate acidified barium reagent to form white barium sulfate. Carbonates release carbon dioxide with a suitable acid; identify that gas using limewater. The exact acid matters because it must not introduce the ion being tested or create a misleading precipitate.

sections.heading: A test result has conditions and limits
sections.body: The presence of one ion may interfere with a test for another, so sequence and acidification are part of the method. A negative result could reflect low concentration or an unsuitable procedure as well as genuine absence. Use the specification’s required ions and the method supplied in an exam. Handle reagents under school supervision; these notes explain observations rather than authorise unsupervised chemical testing.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Halogens, displacement reactions and redox evidence

sections.heading: Connect Group 7 properties to electron gain
sections.body: Halogens are non-metal elements that form diatomic molecules and commonly gain one electron to form halide ions. Their reactivity decreases down the group in the school comparison. As the atoms become larger and shielding increases, the nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly despite the higher nuclear charge. State the competition between these effects rather than reasoning from proton number alone. Distinguish chlorine, Cl₂, from chloride, Cl⁻: one is an element molecule and the other is an ion.

sections.heading: Predict a displacement from relative reactivity
sections.body: A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from its halide solution under suitable conditions. Chlorine can oxidise bromide ions to bromine, while bromine does not displace chlorine from chloride. A proposed equation should be checked against the reactivity order before balancing. If no reaction is predicted, do not manufacture a balanced-looking displacement equation. Observation wording must identify the change in the given system, because starting colours, solvent and concentration can affect the appearance.

sections.heading: Use ionic equations to expose electron transfer
sections.body: For chlorine and bromide, the ionic equation is Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Bromide ions lose electrons and are oxidised; chlorine molecules gain electrons and are reduced. Spectator ions such as sodium are omitted because they are unchanged by the reaction. A halogen acts as an oxidising agent when it accepts electrons from another species. Oxidation and reduction occur together: the electrons lost by one species are gained by the other.

sections.heading: Interpret colour changes with controls
sections.body: A colour change can support product formation, but interpretation requires knowledge of what was present before mixing. Use separate reference samples and the specified solvent where a practical includes partitioning between layers. Do not identify an unknown halogen by smelling it. Compare solutions under the same conditions and record both positive changes and no-change results. A series of displacement observations can establish a reactivity order, but one successful reaction alone establishes only a particular comparison between two halogens.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Energy changes and reaction rates

sections.heading: Follow the energy balance
sections.body: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions absorb it. Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy. Estimate enthalpy change as total energy needed to break reactant bonds minus energy released forming product bonds. A catalyst changes activation energy but does not change the energy difference between reactants and products.

sections.heading: Use collision theory to explain a change in rate
sections.body: Reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy and suitable orientation. Higher concentration or gas pressure increases collision frequency. Higher temperature increases particle speed and the fraction of collisions exceeding activation energy. Greater exposed surface area makes more particles available. A catalyst offers an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is regenerated overall.

sections.heading: Make a fair rate measurement
sections.body: Measure gas volume, mass loss or another appropriate change over time. Control other conditions and repeat trials. The slope of a quantity-time curve gives rate; a tangent gives instantaneous rate. A curve flattening means the measurable change has stopped, not that particles have stopped moving. Distinguish faster completion from a greater final quantity, which depends on reacting amounts.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In simple calorimetry, q = mcΔT estimates energy transferred to the measured liquid. To calculate a molar energy change, divide by the moles corresponding to the stated reaction basis and assign the sign from the system’s energy transfer. Heat loss to surroundings and heating the apparatus commonly reduce the measured liquid temperature change, affecting the result. A rate experiment may instead measure time for a fixed visible change; 1/time is then a comparative rate measure under the stated conditions, rather than a universal rate with units of amount per second.

topics.tip: A higher temperature is not explained only by more collisions; mention the larger fraction with enough energy.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Reversible reactions and equilibrium

sections.heading: An equilibrium is still active
sections.body: A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions. In a closed system, a dynamic equilibrium is reached when forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. Reactant and product concentrations remain constant, but are not necessarily equal. Material must not continuously escape if the equilibrium model is to remain appropriate.

sections.heading: A changed condition favours a response
sections.body: Increasing a reactant concentration tends to favour the direction consuming it. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, where the gaseous mole totals differ. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction. Use the balanced equation and the thermal direction together; a memorised slogan without the relevant details is incomplete.

sections.heading: Industry balances several objectives
sections.body: Conditions that maximise equilibrium yield may produce an impractically slow rate. Industrial choices also consider energy, equipment, separation and recycling. A catalyst speeds both forward and reverse processes and allows equilibrium to be reached sooner, but does not alter equilibrium composition at the same temperature. When evaluating operating conditions, separate yield effects from rate effects.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A change in pressure only shifts a gaseous equilibrium through this argument when the balanced sides have different gas-mole totals. Compressing an equilibrium with equal gaseous mole totals does not favour one direction by that rule. Temperature must be related to the exothermic or endothermic direction; treating temperature as just another concentration can produce a wrong conclusion. The concentration-time graph after a disturbance should settle to new constant values once equal forward and reverse rates are re-established. Those final values need not match each other or the original values.

topics.tip: A catalyst changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not the equilibrium yield.

topics.title: Calorimetry and uncertainty in energy measurements

sections.heading: Define the system and the measured change
sections.body: A simple reaction calorimeter commonly measures the temperature change of a solution. Approximate heat transferred using q = mcΔT, stating assumptions about density, heat capacity and heat losses. The solution gaining heat corresponds to the reaction transferring energy out. A positive solution temperature rise therefore does not mean the reaction’s enthalpy change is positive.

sections.heading: Scale to a stated amount of reaction
sections.body: Use moles of the appropriate limiting reactant and the equation’s reaction basis when calculating a molar energy change. Convert joules to kilojoules consistently. An approximate water heat capacity must not be mixed with an incompatible mass unit. For combustion, heat absorbed by water is only a portion of the fuel’s total transferred energy in a simple open experiment.

sections.heading: Explain realistic limitations
sections.body: Heat escaping to the surroundings, energy absorbed by the container, incomplete combustion and evaporation can each influence the result. Name the mechanism and explain its likely effect rather than saying human error. Insulation and a lid can reduce some losses but introduce their own practical considerations. Repeat measurements estimate consistency; they do not automatically correct a systematic error present in every trial.

sections.heading: Choose a measurable change
sections.body: A reaction rate can be investigated by gas volume, loss of mass or time to a specified visual change. Each method measures a particular consequence of reaction and has different limitations. A gas syringe can measure accumulated gas, but leaks and delayed connection reduce the measured amount. A balance measures mass lost when gas escapes, so its interpretation depends on which species leave and whether evaporation also occurs.

sections.heading: Control the comparison
sections.body: For a concentration investigation, keep relevant quantities such as reactant form, temperature and total liquid volume appropriately controlled. For surface area, use the same reactant mass while changing particle size. Record sufficient points to show the early steep region and later plateau. Compare initial gradients to investigate rate, while final gas volumes reflect reacting amounts and limiting reagents rather than rate alone.

sections.heading: Use gradients with units
sections.body: Mean rate is change in measured quantity divided by time interval. Instantaneous rate uses a tangent to a curve at the stated time. Draw a sufficiently large gradient triangle and read both axes carefully. For time-to-endpoint methods, reciprocal time can compare runs with the same endpoint. A catalyst can make completion earlier without changing the theoretical final product amount from fixed starting quantities.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Dynamic equilibrium and balancing yield against rate

sections.heading: Separate reversible change from dynamic equilibrium
sections.body: A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions under suitable conditions. In a closed system, forward and reverse reaction rates may eventually become equal, producing dynamic equilibrium. The reactions continue at the particle level even though macroscopic concentrations remain constant. Equal rates do not require equal concentrations of reactants and products. Closing the system matters because removing a gas or allowing a reactant to escape can prevent the stated equilibrium from being established or maintained.

sections.heading: Predict concentration and pressure responses
sections.body: When a concentration is changed, the equilibrium system responds in a direction that tends to oppose that imposed change. Adding a reactant can favour its consumption and increase equilibrium product yield in the relevant reaction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules when the equation has unequal gaseous coefficients. Count only gaseous species for this comparison. If gas-molecule numbers are equal on both sides, pressure does not favour either side in this simple model. Distinguish a shift in equilibrium composition from an immediate concentration increase caused simply by compression.

sections.heading: Relate temperature to the reaction direction
sections.body: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, while decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction. First identify which direction is exothermic in the given equation. For an exothermic forward reaction, a lower temperature can improve equilibrium yield but slow the approach to equilibrium. A catalyst speeds both directions and allows equilibrium to be reached sooner; it does not change the equilibrium composition at the same temperature. A faster reaction and a higher equilibrium yield are therefore different advantages.

sections.heading: Explain an industrial compromise with evidence
sections.body: For ammonia synthesis, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic in the forward direction. Higher pressure favours ammonia because four gas molecules become two. Lower temperature favours equilibrium yield but may make the reaction too slow for economical production. A catalyst and an intermediate operating temperature provide a practical rate, while pressure is limited by equipment, energy and safety costs. Removing ammonia and recycling unreacted gases can improve overall production. A balanced evaluation connects each condition to rate, yield and engineering cost rather than declaring that every variable should simply be maximised.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Crude oil, alkanes and alkenes

sections.heading: Separate a mixture before using it
sections.body: Crude oil is a mixture, mainly of hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation separates fractions by different boiling ranges. Smaller molecules generally have lower boiling points and greater volatility; longer chains are generally more viscous. Fractions are mixtures with similar properties rather than single pure compounds. Complete combustion needs sufficient oxygen; incomplete combustion can create carbon monoxide and soot.

sections.heading: Homologous series organise chemical behaviour
sections.body: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only carbon-carbon single bonds; open-chain alkanes have general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Alkenes have a carbon-carbon double bond and, for one double bond in an open chain, formula CₙH₂ₙ. Alkenes undergo addition reactions. Bromine water is decolourised by a suitable unsaturated compound, providing a test for the double bond in this context.

sections.heading: Cracking changes the product balance
sections.body: Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, often including an alkane and an alkene, using heat and an appropriate catalyst or other specified conditions. It supplies useful fuels and chemical feedstocks. Balance atoms in any proposed equation. Structural formulae show bonding and can distinguish structural isomers, which share a molecular formula but have different connectivity.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A homologous series shares a functional pattern and general formula while successive members differ by a CH₂ unit. Chain length changes physical properties gradually, while the functional group strongly influences reaction type. Alkanes can react with halogens by substitution under suitable light conditions; alkenes undergo addition at a carbon-carbon double bond. A displayed or structural formula must show a chemically valid bonding arrangement, with carbon making four bonds in the usual neutral structures. Two compounds with the same molecular formula can have different connectivity and therefore be structural isomers.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Alcohols, acids, esters and polymers

sections.heading: Functional groups change behaviour
sections.body: Alcohols contain the −OH functional group; carboxylic acids contain −COOH. Ethanol can be made by fermentation of sugars using yeast under suitable anaerobic conditions, or by adding steam to ethene using an appropriate catalyst and industrial conditions. Oxidising ethanol can form ethanoic acid. Describing an alcohol as simply a hydrocarbon is incorrect because it also contains oxygen.

sections.heading: Esterification links an acid to an alcohol
sections.body: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid can react to form an ester and water, usually with acid catalysis and warming. Ester names combine the alcohol-derived alkyl group with the acid-derived carboxylate group. Many esters have useful aromas or solvent properties. Conditions, separation and equilibrium affect practical yield; the reaction equation alone does not describe a complete manufacturing process.

sections.heading: Small molecules become macromolecules
sections.body: Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers by opening their carbon-carbon double bonds. The repeating unit must preserve every atom of the monomer, with continuation bonds through brackets. Condensation polymerisation links monomers with suitable functional groups and eliminates a small molecule. Disposal choices include reuse, recycling and energy recovery, each with limitations including sorting, contamination, emissions and persistence.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: To draw an addition-polymer repeat unit, retain the monomer’s side groups, change the double bond to a single bond and show continuation bonds through both sides of the brackets. A condensation polymer has linking groups related to its monomers’ functional groups and forms a small molecule in the linking reaction. A polymer can be chemically resistant yet difficult to recycle because of mixed grades, additives or contamination. In ethanol production, compare fermentation and hydration using feedstock, purity, conditions, rate and separation rather than assuming one method is best under every industrial constraint.

sections.heading: A formula must show the intended connectivity
sections.body: A molecular formula gives atom counts but not a unique arrangement. Structural and displayed formulae communicate how atoms connect. Check carbon’s usual valency of four, oxygen’s of two and hydrogen’s of one in the neutral compounds studied. sections.heading: Use the functional group in the name
sections.body: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid can form an ester and water under suitable catalysed conditions. The alcohol gives the ester’s alkyl part; the acid gives its carboxylate part. Methanol and ethanoic acid therefore produce methyl ethanoate. The functional group determines much of the chemistry, while carbon-chain length also influences physical properties. The OH within a carboxyl group is not a separate free hydroxide ion.

sections.body: In addition polymerisation, open the alkene double bond to show connections to neighbouring repeat units and retain side groups. Include continuation bonds through brackets. topics.title: Addition and condensation polymers from their structures

sections.heading: Recognise an addition monomer
sections.body: An alkene contains a carbon–carbon double bond. In addition polymerisation, many suitable monomers join as the double bond opens to form links in a long chain. The atoms in each monomer are retained in the polymer repeat units; a small molecule is not eliminated in the simple addition process. The carbon backbone of the repeat unit has single bonds, with the original side groups attached to the corresponding carbons. Do not remove hydrogen atoms without a structural reason.

sections.heading: Move between monomer and repeat unit
sections.body: To derive a repeat unit from an alkene, replace the double bond with a single backbone bond and show continuation bonds through brackets with n outside. To infer a monomer, identify a suitable two-carbon repeat pattern and restore the double bond between those backbone carbons, keeping side groups attached correctly. A repeat unit is not an isolated molecule with ordinary completed end groups. Its open bonds indicate continuation into the rest of the chain. Check the atom counts and valencies before finalising a structure.

sections.heading: Explain condensation through functional groups
sections.body: Condensation polymerisation requires monomers with suitable reactive groups at two positions so a long chain can grow. For a polyester, alcohol and carboxylic-acid groups react to form ester links, with a small molecule such as water eliminated in the school model. The ester linkage contains the arrangement –COO– in the chain. Identify the linkage and the two functional-group types rather than relying solely on a polymer name. Unlike simple addition polymerisation, not every atom in the reacting monomers remains in the main polymer product.

sections.heading: Evaluate use and disposal using structure
sections.body: Polymer properties depend on chain arrangement, side groups, intermolecular attractions and cross-linking, so not all polymers have identical flexibility or thermal behaviour. Disposal choices include reuse, suitable recycling, energy recovery and landfill, each with material and infrastructure constraints. A polymer being chemically recyclable in principle does not show that local collection and processing exist. Biodegradability depends on structure and environmental conditions; it is not a promise that every discarded polymer disappears rapidly without harmful consequences.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Motion graphs and acceleration

sections.heading: Describe change with quantities and directions
sections.body: Distance measures total path length, while displacement is change in position with direction. Speed is distance divided by time; velocity includes direction. Average speed uses total distance divided by total time. Acceleration is change in velocity per unit time and can describe a change of direction even if speed is constant.

sections.heading: Gradients and areas have physical meanings
sections.body: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity. On a velocity-time graph, gradient is acceleration and signed area is displacement. A flat velocity-time section represents constant velocity, whereas a flat displacement-time section represents rest. Use a tangent to estimate a gradient at a particular instant on a curve, showing the triangle used.

sections.heading: Uniform acceleration is a restricted model
sections.body: For constant acceleration, v = u + at and v² = u² + 2as. Choose the equation that contains your known quantities and the desired unknown. State a positive direction before substituting signed values. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. Stopping distance combines thinking and braking distances; fatigue, speed and road conditions affect different stages.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A curved displacement-time graph has a changing gradient and therefore changing velocity. A straight sloping velocity-time segment represents uniform acceleration, even if the velocity itself is negative. For a journey with several stages, add the distances and times before calculating average speed. In experimental motion work, light gates or video measurements reduce some timing limitations, but the physical quantity still depends on gate spacing, flag length or scale calibration. State the model assumptions when applying constant-acceleration equations, because a single average acceleration does not prove the acceleration was uniform throughout.

topics.tip: A descending velocity-time line can indicate slowing down or speeding up in the negative direction; examine the sign.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Forces, moments, momentum and springs

sections.heading: Resultant force changes motion
sections.body: Force is a vector. A zero resultant force means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity. For a constant mass, F = ma. Weight is the gravitational force mg, whereas mass measures the amount of matter and resistance to acceleration. Free-body diagrams show forces on one object; action-reaction pairs act on different objects.

sections.heading: Turning and balancing
sections.body: A moment is force multiplied by perpendicular distance to the pivot. For rotational equilibrium, clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance. A body’s centre of gravity is where its weight can be treated as acting. Stability depends on the centre of gravity and the support base. A spring follows F = kx only within its linear range; extension is the increase from original length.

sections.heading: Momentum accounts for interactions
sections.body: Momentum is mass × velocity. In an isolated interaction, total momentum is conserved. A resultant force equals rate of change of momentum; increasing collision time can reduce mean force for the same momentum change. During terminal fall, resistive force grows until it balances weight and acceleration becomes zero. Energy transfers may still continue while terminal speed is maintained.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For an object in equilibrium, both the resultant force and resultant moment must be zero. Balancing moments about a convenient pivot removes the moment of any force acting through that pivot, but the force still matters in the overall force balance. A spring constant is the gradient of a force-extension graph in the linear range. The area under that graph is elastic energy transferred; for a linear spring this is ½Fx = ½kx². In a collision, use one positive direction consistently before applying conservation of momentum.

topics.tip: Use a signed velocity change when an object reverses direction.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Measuring motion and evaluating timing

sections.heading: Define the measured interval
sections.body: Average speed uses distance travelled during a measured interval. In a light-gate experiment, a known interrupting flag length and blockage time can estimate the object’s speed at the gate. Between two gates, use their separation and the travel time for average speed over that region. These are different intervals and must not be confused. A video method needs a distance scale and known frame interval.

sections.heading: Calculate and compare acceleration
sections.body: Estimate acceleration from a change in measured velocity divided by elapsed time. For motion on a slope, identify forces and the intended control variables. A constant average acceleration over one interval does not prove the acceleration is unchanged at every instant. Repeated trials can reveal variability, while calibration of length and timing affects systematic accuracy.

sections.heading: Judge improvements specifically
sections.body: Reducing human reaction-time effects can be useful for short intervals, but an automatic instrument still needs correct setup. An incorrectly measured flag length biases every speed calculated from it. Increasing travel distance can make manual timing relatively less sensitive to a fixed timing uncertainty, provided the motion remains appropriate for the model. Record units and keep enough significant figures during intermediate calculations.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Momentum, collisions and safety through stopping time

sections.heading: Treat momentum as a signed quantity
sections.body: Momentum equals mass multiplied by velocity. Its SI unit is kg m/s, and its direction follows velocity. Choose a positive direction before calculating in a one-dimensional problem. An object travelling in the opposite direction has a negative velocity and negative momentum in that convention. Add signed momenta for a system rather than adding every speed as a positive number. A stationary object has zero momentum in the chosen reference frame, even though it still has mass.

sections.heading: State the system for conservation
sections.body: Total momentum is conserved when the resultant external force on the chosen system is zero, or negligible over the short interaction. In a collision between two carts, the carts exert forces on each other, but those are internal to the two-cart system. Conservation does not mean that each cart’s momentum stays unchanged. For objects that stick together, use their combined mass and common final velocity. A collision may conserve total momentum while kinetic energy is transferred into thermal energy, sound or deformation.

sections.heading: Connect force to the time of momentum change
sections.body: The average resultant force is change in momentum divided by the time taken. If an occupant comes to rest from the same initial velocity, increasing the stopping time reduces the magnitude of the average force for the same momentum change. Seat belts, airbags and crumple zones can increase the stopping time or distance in appropriate ways. They do not make the initial momentum disappear before the interaction. Use force direction consistently: a braking force acts opposite the original motion when the object slows down.

sections.heading: Check the interpretation and the model
sections.body: After solving a collision, a negative final velocity means motion opposite to the chosen positive direction; it is not automatically an impossible answer. Check the momentum before and after numerically. Distinguish a two-body collision from a longer stopping process where a road or wall exerts an important external force. If a question asks about kinetic energy, calculate it separately using one-half mv². Do not infer kinetic-energy conservation solely because the momentum equation balanced.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Moments, centre of gravity and stable equilibrium

sections.heading: Use perpendicular distance from the pivot
sections.body: The moment of a force about a pivot equals force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. The distance is not automatically the full length of the handle or the distance to the point where the force is applied. A force whose line of action passes through the pivot has zero moment about it. Label clockwise and anticlockwise effects on a sketch. Moment is measured in N m, which describes a turning effect; it should not be confused with work simply because the units have a similar product form.

sections.heading: Apply both conditions for a balanced object
sections.body: For rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment about the same point. For full static equilibrium, resultant force must also be zero. Choosing a pivot through an unknown support force can simplify the moment equation because that force then has no moment about the pivot. Include the weight of the beam or object if it is relevant; a uniform beam’s weight acts at its midpoint in the usual school model. Give every force its correct distance and direction.

sections.heading: Relate centre of gravity to toppling
sections.body: The centre of gravity is the point through which an object’s weight can be considered to act. An object on a base tends to topple when the line of action of its weight falls outside the supporting base, producing an overturning moment about an edge. A wider base or lower centre of gravity can improve stability against tilting. These are geometric and force relationships, not claims that a heavier object can never topple. Compare objects under the same loading and surface conditions.

sections.heading: Evaluate a measurement of turning effects
sections.body: A practical may balance known masses at measured distances along a beam. Measure the distance to the force’s line of action, use appropriate mass-to-weight conversion and check that the pivot has low friction. The beam’s own weight and any hanger masses can affect the result. Repeating the arrangement or reversing sides can expose systematic differences. A diagram with distances and units makes the method assessable, while merely saying “balance it” does not explain which quantities are controlled or compared.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Charge, current, voltage and circuit rules

sections.heading: Current is moving charge
sections.body: Charge flow is Q = It. Current has the same value through components in series; currents entering a junction sum to those leaving. Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, V = E/Q. In parallel branches the potential difference is equal. An ammeter is placed in series and a voltmeter in parallel with the component being measured.

sections.heading: Components respond differently
sections.body: An ohmic resistor has constant resistance at constant temperature. A filament lamp’s resistance increases as its temperature rises. A diode conducts much more readily in one direction. The resistance of a thermistor commonly decreases as temperature rises; an LDR’s resistance decreases as light level rises. Interpret each component using its current-voltage behaviour, not by assuming every graph is a straight line.

sections.heading: Resistance and power in networks
sections.body: For series resistors, add resistances. Parallel paths reduce the total resistance compared with any individual branch. V = IR relates a component’s potential difference, current and resistance. Electrical power is P = VI and, for a resistive component, P = I²R. Energy transferred is E = Pt. Match units: watts and seconds give joules.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In parallel branches, equal potential difference does not imply equal current unless the branch resistances are equal. For two resistors, the reciprocal relation 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ gives a combined resistance below either individual resistance. In a potential divider, the fraction of supply voltage across a series component depends on its share of the total resistance. Measurements must distinguish a component’s current-voltage behaviour from changes caused by heating. Connect equipment correctly and keep current low enough to avoid unwanted temperature changes when investigating an ohmic resistor.

topics.tip: Current is not used up as it travels around a circuit.
topics.formula: Q = It; V = IR; P = VI; E = Pt

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Mains safety and static electricity

sections.heading: Protect the user when something goes wrong
sections.body: A live conductor is at an alternating potential relative to earth; neutral provides the return path. An earth conductor connects exposed conducting parts to earth so a fault can create a large current and operate protective devices. A fuse melts when excessive current heats it. Double-insulated equipment has appropriate insulating barriers and does not rely on an earth wire for exposed metal protection.

sections.heading: Choose protective ratings sensibly
sections.body: Calculate normal current from P/V before choosing the next suitable fuse rating above it, allowing for the specified equipment characteristics. Overloading sockets can overheat wiring. Electrical energy billing commonly uses kilowatt-hours: multiply power in kilowatts by time in hours. A kilowatt-hour is an energy unit, not power per hour.

sections.heading: Charge transfer creates static effects
sections.body: Rubbing insulating materials can transfer electrons. Losing electrons leaves a positive charge; gaining them leaves a negative charge. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. A charged object can attract a neutral object by redistributing its charges. Static build-up may cause sparks, so fuel handling and other sensitive processes use earthing and suitable precautions.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An alternating supply reverses direction repeatedly; a direct supply has a fixed direction. A fuse is chosen to tolerate normal operation while protecting against excessive current in a suitable circuit. The live path must be interrupted by the protective or switching device where specified, because leaving internal parts connected to live can remain dangerous. Static induction redistributes charges within a nearby object without requiring net charge transfer to it. When a conductor is earthed, electrons may flow to or from Earth according to the surrounding charge arrangement.

topics.tip: An earth wire is a fault-protection route; it should not normally carry the appliance current.

sections.heading: Build the measurement circuit
sections.body: Use an ammeter in series with the component and a voltmeter across it. A suitable variable supply or resistance controls the operating point. Take paired voltage and current readings and record the direction of each quantity consistently. Reverse polarity where the approved circuit and component permit it to investigate the other branch. Protect the component from excessive current and follow the school’s circuit instructions.

sections.heading: Recognise the shapes
sections.body: An ohmic resistor at constant temperature gives a straight current-voltage graph through the origin. A filament lamp’s curve becomes less steep as it heats and resistance increases, when current is plotted vertically against voltage. A diode shows strong directional behaviour, with relatively little current in reverse under the normal intended operating conditions. Axis choice matters when interpreting steepness.

sections.heading: Separate component behaviour from experimental effects
sections.body: Heating is the intended reason for the lamp’s changing resistance, but can be an unwanted confound in a resistor investigation. Allow suitable cooling or limit current where needed. Calculate V/I at a point to obtain that operating resistance; do not automatically call the tangent gradient resistance on every graph. Check instrument ranges, connections and zero readings before attributing an unexpected curve to new physics.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Wave behaviour, sound and the electromagnetic spectrum

sections.heading: Track the oscillation and the energy separately
sections.body: Waves transfer energy without net transport of the medium. In transverse waves the oscillation is perpendicular to travel; in longitudinal waves it is parallel. Amplitude measures maximum displacement, wavelength measures repeat distance, frequency counts cycles per second and period is time per cycle. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

sections.heading: At boundaries, follow what changes
sections.body: Reflection returns a wave from a boundary; refraction occurs when wave speed changes between media. Frequency remains fixed by the source during refraction, while wavelength changes. Diffraction spreads waves around obstacles or through openings and is greatest when wavelength and opening width are comparable. Sound needs a medium; pitch relates to frequency and loudness to amplitude.

sections.heading: One spectrum, different interactions
sections.body: Electromagnetic waves are transverse and have the same speed in vacuum. Increasing frequency runs from radio through microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-rays to gamma radiation. Use depends on penetration, absorption and energy transfer. Ionising radiation can damage cells; exposure decisions weigh dose, shielding, distance and benefits. Infrared is associated with thermal emission and absorption, not with a special category of heat particles.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: At a boundary, a wave’s frequency remains controlled by its source, so a speed change produces a corresponding wavelength change. Echo measurements use a return journey: divide the product of speed and time by two to find the reflecting distance. Increasing sound amplitude generally increases loudness; increasing frequency raises pitch. Different electromagnetic bands interact differently with matter, which explains uses such as radio communication, thermal imaging and medical imaging. The label ionising concerns sufficient energy to remove bound electrons in relevant interactions, not simply whether a wave travels through a solid.

topics.tip: Frequency does not change just because a wave enters a different medium.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Refraction, total internal reflection and lenses

sections.heading: Draw from the normal
sections.body: Angles of incidence and refraction are measured from the normal, not the surface. A ray entering a slower medium generally bends towards the normal; entering a faster medium generally bends away. The refractive index compares speeds and, for air-to-material geometry, relates sin i to sin r. Keep calculator angles in degrees for school ray calculations.

sections.heading: A critical angle sets a boundary
sections.body: Total internal reflection requires travel from a higher-index medium toward a lower-index medium and an incidence angle greater than the critical angle. At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary. Optical fibres use repeated internal reflection, although real systems also have attenuation and manufacturing constraints. Reflection below the critical angle is not total internal reflection.

sections.heading: Lenses produce images by ray geometry
sections.body: A converging lens brings parallel rays towards a focal point. Draw a ray parallel to the principal axis that passes through the far focus and a ray through the optical centre that continues essentially undeviated in the thin-lens model. Where real rays meet, a real image forms; where their backward extensions meet, the image is virtual. Magnification is image size divided by object size.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A real image can be formed on a screen because light rays actually converge there. A virtual image is located where backward extensions of rays meet, and cannot be projected directly onto a screen in the same way. A converging lens can form either type depending on object position. Ray diagrams must use a clear principal axis and accurately placed focal points. At total internal reflection, the critical-angle condition concerns a higher-index to lower-index boundary; simply making any incidence angle large does not guarantee it.

topics.tip: Total internal reflection cannot occur when the ray first enters a higher-index medium from air.
